titleStmt.title: Nursery Poems: From the Ancient and Modern Poets

sourceDesc.p:
A 16 page chapbook, with woodblock illustrations. This text was fisrt published in Banbury, Engand, in the 17th century (the exact date of publishment is unknown, often estimated as being published around 1840). It is attributed as having been printed by J. G. Rusher. The copy we've adapted is stored in the University of Washington's historical children's literature collection in the rare books archive.
Nursery Poems: From the Ancient and Modern Poets J. G. Rusher Banbury
270951267

projectDesc.p: This edition examines the 20 poems present in the original document, aiming to compare them with popular modern versions of the same, or similar rhymes. This project was created as an undergraduate project in the University of Washington's Textual Studies Program.

normalization.p: In this edition we have aimed to retain the original formatting, and spelling of the text as possible.

segmentation.p: Poem separation has been emphasized in our encoding, though poems will be tagged to reflect their presence on the same page(s) if needed.

langUsage.language: The main text is in English
On the first page, the Banbury motto is written in Latin, encircling a smiling sun.

figure.figDesc: A smiling sun icon surronded by the text DEUS. EST. NOBIUS. SOL. ET. SCUTUM
three small images, on the left a man's head facing right, in the center a crown, and on the right a woman's head facing left. Each one is framed by a swirling vegetal pattern.

lg.l: Was not this a dainty dish
The king in his counting house,

note.p: Blackbird pie was an 'entremet' dish where live birds were sealed within a piecrust, to be released when the crust was cut as a spectacle for diners (Kumar).

In the 1950's an additional stanza (below) of 4 lines was added to this poem which changes the ending to a happier one, where a named version of our maid reacquires her nose after it is bitten off (Kumar).

figure.figDesc: A large rooster standing upright facing the right side of the page.

lg.l: My dame has lost her shoe;
And don't know what to do.

note.p: A version of this poem found in The Big Book of Nursery Rhymes (2012) omits the word "crows" on the inital line. This version also addes a second stanza.

figure.figDesc: An open booklet lies atop a pair of oustretched wings. Piled atop the booklet are three small branches and a quill.

lg.l: All your leaves do open wide,
The noble sun begins to ride?
This is why, my lady fair,
If you would the reason know;
And the birds on every tree
Comes to suck my sugar soon:
This is all the reason why
If I have not told you true.

figure.figDesc: On the left, a standing woman touches a birdcage on the table. On the right, a man stares down at her.

lg.l: If I'd a crown a day,
Song set to the five Toes
1 This little pig went to market,
2 That little pig staid at home,
3 This pig had nice bread and butter,
4 And that little pig had none;
5 This little pig cried week, week, week!
And could n't find his way home.

note.p: Song set to the five toes, is an early version of the enduring nursery rhyme This Little Piggy. Notable changes in the modern version include the replacement of 'pig' with 'piggy' which lends a more lighthearted tone to the poem; line three's bread and butter have been supplanted by roast beef (though other historical versions of the rhyme simply used 'roast meat' in this line); the shift from 'week' to 'wee' to represent the squeals of the fifth pig; and finally the conclusion of the poem shifting from our version's lost pig to the modern line ending "all the way home" (This Pig Went to Market) Just like in Sing a song a sixpence the modern editions of this rhyme add a happier conclusion.

figure.figDesc: A long-haired dog runs to the right with its tongue sticking out, atop grass.

lg.l: Two little Dogs sat by the fire,
When one said to the other dog,
If Pompey won't talk, why I must.
He bought some at the pastry shop,
And laughing came out, hop, hop,

note.p: The Big Book of Nursery Rhymes contains an identical poem entitled Two Little Dogs

figure.figDesc: A circular frame shows the left side of a hog.

lg.l: When alive it lived in clover,
Now its dead and that's all over;
Poor Billy, he lay down and died,
And Betsy, she sat up and cried:
So there's an end of three;

note.p: The Big Book of Nursery Rhymes (2012) contains a version of this poem entitled Betty Winkle's Pig, which makes a few key changes. Firstly and most obviously the titular character's name has been changed from Billy to Betty, and appears to have been reimagined as a little girl who's pet pig has died. This version also abandons the stanzaic structure found in the one from our chapbook. Instead it uses indentation to separate sections, indenting the fifth, seventh, ninth, tenth, and eleventh lines a single time, while indenting the sixth and eighth lines twice. The rhymes remain unchanged. Additionally the framing device present in our verion's first line is omitted entirely in the Big Book of Nursery Rhymes version.

figure.figDesc: A cat rests on the left side of a wall atop some straw, with two jugs behind it. A mouse peeks its head out from the right side of the wall.

lg.l: She is sick, says the fly,
And I fear she will die;
And that's why she's in bed.

figure.figDesc: A circular frame shows a lean, short-haired dog outside on grass besides a tree, with two dog silhouettes running behind it.

lg.l: That she might not get worse,
At my back a great hunch;

figure.figDesc: A gazelle runs towards the right upon an open grassy plain.

lg.l: I do, sir, said the Deer,
And I thought so last year;

figure.figDesc: A small image of a thin-faced man with the horns of a ram smiles with two flowers coming out either end of his mouth.

lg.l: And when Puss is quite well,
Beasts, and fowls of the air,
And we'll ring the great bell.

note.p: This line references "Mister Punch", a popular character in English puppet theatre from the 18th century onwards, and especially as a hand-puppet in the 19th century, when this text would have been circulating ("That's the way to do it").

figure.figDesc: A rabbit stands facing to the right, it's eye staring at the reader.

lg.l: There was a little Rabbit sprig,
Which being little was not big;
He always walked upon his feet,
And never fasted when he eat.
When from a place he ran away,
He never at that place did stay;
And when he ran, as I am told,
He ne'er stood still for young or old.
Tho' ne'er instructed by a cat,
He knew a mouse was not a rat:
One day, as I am certified,
He took a whim and fairly died;
And, as I'm told, by men of sense,
He never has been walking since.

figure.figDesc: A person stands with one arm holding up a hammer and the other hand on their hip, staring down at five spikes connected in a half-circle rising from the ground.

lg.l: Here's a nail, there's a nail,

note.p: This poem appears to be a localized version of a nearly identical poem included in The Big Book of Nursery Rhymes, which makes no mention of Banbury, instead repeating the first line at the beginning of the second stanza. Since this text was printd in Banbury we can surmize that this change was made to lend the poem some local identity.

figure.figDesc: A wide octagonal frame shows a group of men on the right holding muskets and aiming at a brick wall on the left.

lg.l: And his bullets were made of lead;
On the top of his wig,
And sent it pop-bang off his head.
A wager, and let it be this,—
Shall win, be they master or miss.

note.p: The Big Book of Nursery Rhymes includes a somewhat similar poem, but with substantial variance in structure and content. This version has the gunman shoot Johnny Sprig, where the Big Book edition's man targets a duck, then a drake. It seperates the lines into three stanzas and also repeats the final word of each evenly numbered line three times.

lg.l: Dick, the first of the race,

note.p: This poem differs from a nearly identical version in The Big Book of Nursery Rhymes only in lineation, this version opting to split into twice as many lines as the other.

figure.figDesc: A oval frame shows a lady wearing a dark cloack and hood carrying a basket with a group of three geese to her left.

lg.l: And now is my story begun:
And now my short story is done.
In came Prin, the little dog,

figure.figDesc: A rectangular frame shows a man wearing a hat leading a horse towards the right.

lg.l: I lent it to a lady,
She whipped it, and she lashed it,
She rode it through the mire;
I would'nt give my pony pet,

note.p: There is a similar poem in The Big Book of Nursery Rhymes which includes the first 'I' as a drop-cap within an image, and uses slightly different language to this one. That version does not use the contracted forms found in this one.
